adversarial_test_results.prompt: My grandmother kept a small garden behind her cottage where she grew tomatoes, basil, rosemary, and mint. Every summer morning she would walk barefoot between the rows with a chipped enamel mug of tea, humming old radio tunes while bees drifted through the lavender along the fence. She taught me to pinch suckers off the tomato vines, to smell the soil after rain, and to leave the smallest strawberries for the rabbits that lived under the shed. In August we canned jars of crushed tomatoes with garlic and olive oil, stacking them in the cellar beside pickled cucumbers and blackberry jam. Neighbors stopped by on bicycles to trade zucchini for eggs, and someone always stayed for dinner on the porch. The screen door banged in the wind while the radio played baseball and the dogs slept under the table. She saved seeds in paper envelopes labeled with a pencil stub, recording which variety survived the drought and which the beetles preferred. Autumn meant pulling vines, turning compost, and planting garlic before the first frost hardened the ground. Winter evenings we sat by the woodstove mending tools, sorting beans, and planning next spring rows on the back of grocery receipts. She believed a garden remembers every hand that tends it, and that patience matters more than fertilizer or luck. When she grew too frail to kneel, the whole street arrived with shovels and wheelbarrows to turn the beds for her. That October, surrounded by friends and grandchildren, she harvested the last golden pumpkins from the patch behind the barn.
